newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka faces tough balancing act in '97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka faces tough balancing act in '97 budget.

text.p: Faced with an escalating war against Tamil Tiger separatist rebels and a slowing economy, the Sri Lankan government has a tough task in balancing its budget for next year, analysts said on Sunday.
"The government will have to do a delicate balancing act," said a government economist who declined to be identified. "It will have a difficult time in raising revenue."
He said the economic slowdown was a result of intensified fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam and a drought which caused severe power cuts earlier this year.
Inflation is expected to hit 16 percent at year end, up from 7.7 percent last year, while high interest rates forced up by heavy government borrowing to fund the war are hurting business.
"Inflation has now come to stay," said Arjuna Mahendran of Crosby Lanka. "The government probably will try to focus more on job creation."
Growth in industrial exports and corporate earnings have slowed while foreign reserves are also falling and the stock market is in the doldrums.
Deputy Finance Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris has said the economy is expected to grow four percent this year and bounce back in 1997 to at least last year's growth of 5.5 percent.
Peiris, who will present his budget proposals to parliament in early November, has said he will aim to generate jobs and cut unemployment, which officially stands at 13 percent.
"We understand it is a difficult situation," said Panduka Ambanpola, head of research at brokerage Jardine Fleming HNB.
"Cost cutting is a difficult proposition," he added. "The main areas of revenue are privatisation, borrowing from state banks and monetisation (printing money)."

Economists said the government would be forced to keep capital spending down because of high defence expenditure to fight the rebels demanding independence for minority Tamils in the island's north and east.

Defence spending in calendar 1997 at 44 billion rupees ($786 million) will account for 22 percent of overall spending but be lower than this year's 48 billion rupees, most of which was spent on buying arms and equipment.

Budget estimates presented to parliament last week put overall spending at 283.3 billion rupees, up from 278 billion in 1996, while revenue is pegged at 185.7 billion rupees, up 17 billion rupees from 1996.
The overall budget deficit of 98 billion rupees is expected to be about eight percent of gross domestic product in 1997 compared to nine percent this year.
Crosby's Mahendran said the government's privatisation programme was unlikely to generate the hoped-for revenue.

"I do not think they can get half of it," he said. "Hopefully, a number of large enterprises should come on stream next year, like Sri Lanka Telecom and (national airline) Airlanka, and those revenues will help cut the deficit."
A new goods and services tax, introduced last week to replace the existing business turnover tax, should improve government tax collections, he said.
Peiris said in a recent magazine interview that the government did not plan to cut welfare spending of 15 billion rupees a year but instead target it better to help the most vulnerable.
The government also planned to increase money supply and make easier credit available for small and medium industries to generate employment, Peiris said.
